This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

```text
interface g0/24
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk native vlan 99
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99
 switchport nonegotiate
! show interfaces trunk
```


#### Check your understanding

What happens to native-VLAN traffic on a default 802.1Q Cisco trunk?

- **A.** It is always dropped
- **B.** It is sent untagged
- **C.** It uses UDP encapsulation
- **D.** It is encrypted

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**B. It is sent untagged**

By default, native-VLAN frames are untagged. Some platforms support explicitly tagging the native VLAN.

</details>

Next objective: [2.3 CDP and LLDP discovery](#objective-2-3)

<a id="objective-2-3"></a>

### 2.3 — CDP and LLDP discovery

**Exam target:** Configure and verify.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/2.3) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/2.3/commands)

Neighbor-discovery protocols reveal directly connected devices and ports. They do not show an entire routed topology.

#### Build your understanding

- CDP is Cisco proprietary and Layer 2. LLDP is vendor neutral (IEEE 802.1AB). Both can advertise device identity, port, capabilities and management information.
- Use detailed neighbor output to document cabling and identify a remote management address. A discovered neighbor does not prove all VLANs or IP routes are working.
- Enable discovery where useful and disable it on untrusted ports when policy requires. On IOS, cdp run is global; lldp run enables LLDP; interfaces can control transmit and receive.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 2 · Chapters 13](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Read the advertised fields

Compare device ID, local interface, remote port ID, capabilities, platform and management address. An advertised management address does not prove that current VLANs, routes and filters permit reaching it.

##### Check scope and direction

LLDP transmit and receive can be controlled independently. CDP/LLDP discover directly connected Layer 2 neighbors; LLDP-MED adds endpoint information such as voice policy. Discovery neither authenticates a neighbor nor validates the entire topology.

##### Worked review check

LLDP sees a neighbor but its management IP cannot be pinged. Is discovery disproved?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

No. Layer 2 advertisements can work while management addressing, VLAN membership, routing or security policy prevents IP reachability.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Enable and verify Layer 2 discovery.

**Covered features:** CDP; LLDP; Direct-neighbor documentation.

##### Enable discovery on an infrastructure link

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

CDP is Cisco proprietary; LLDP is vendor neutral. Interface and global settings both matter.

```text
enable
configure terminal
cdp run
lldp run
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/24
 cdp enable
 lldp transmit
 lldp receive
end
```


##### Verify neighbor identity and ports

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

Record the local port, remote port, platform and management address. These protocols reveal direct neighbors rather than a complete routed topology.

```text
show cdp neighbors detail
show lldp neighbors detail
show cdp interface GigabitEthernet1/0/24
show lldp interface GigabitEthernet1/0/24
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- No neighbor: check peer discovery settings, cabling and interface operational state.
- Disable discovery where the intended security policy calls for it; do not blindly disable it on links used for operations or voice.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

```text
show cdp neighbors detail
show lldp neighbors detail
configure terminal
 lldp run
 interface g0/1
  lldp transmit
  lldp receive
```


#### Check your understanding

Which discovery protocol is vendor neutral?

- **A.** CDP
- **B.** LLDP
- **C.** DTP
- **D.** PAgP

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**B. LLDP**

LLDP is standardized by IEEE 802.1AB; CDP is Cisco proprietary.

</details>

Next objective: [2.4 Layer 2 and Layer 3 LACP EtherChannels](#objective-2-4)

<a id="objective-2-4"></a>

### 2.4 — Layer 2 and Layer 3 LACP EtherChannels

**Exam target:** Configure and verify.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/2.4) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/2.4/commands)

EtherChannel bundles compatible links into one logical port-channel for capacity and redundancy.

#### Build your understanding

- LACP active initiates negotiation; passive responds. Active/active and active/passive work; passive/passive does not initiate a bundle.
- Member ports need consistent speed, duplex, access/trunk mode and VLAN settings. Configure the logical port-channel consistently; use show etherchannel summary to inspect bundled and suspended members.
- Load balancing hashes flows over member links. A single flow generally uses one physical member, so a four-link bundle does not make one transfer four times faster. Layer 3 EtherChannels use routed ports and an IP on the port-channel.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 1 · Chapters 10, 18](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-1-9780138229634)

##### Troubleshoot members

Check compatible speed, duplex, negotiation, Layer 2/3 mode and VLAN settings. Individual or suspended members differ from bundled members. A port-channel can exist without every intended member participating; inspect the member flags and both endpoints.

##### Connect bundling to STP and routing

STP treats a Layer 2 port-channel as one logical link. A routed port-channel places the address on the logical interface and uses routed members. Hashing distributes flows; a single flow normally remains limited to one physical member’s bandwidth.

##### Worked review check

Both endpoints use LACP passive. Why does the bundle not negotiate?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

Neither peer initiates negotiation. Set at least one side to active, then verify compatible members and bundled state.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Create LACP bundles at Layer 2 or Layer 3.

**Covered features:** LACP active/passive; Layer 2 EtherChannel; Layer 3 EtherChannel.

##### Build a two-link Layer 2 trunk bundle

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** Both switches — compatible member links required

Use consistent speed, mode, native VLAN and allowed VLANs on members, port-channel and peer. At least one end must be LACP active.

```text
enable
configure terminal
interface range GigabitEthernet1/0/21-22
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30
 channel-group 1 mode active
 no shutdown
exit
interface Port-channel1
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30
end
```


##### Alternative: routed port-channel

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** Layer 3 switches — separate links, not the L2 bundle above

Configure the peer Port-channel2 as 10.0.12.2/30. Physical members have no individual IP address in this example.

```text
enable
configure terminal
ip routing
interface range GigabitEthernet1/0/19-20
 no switchport
 channel-group 2 mode active
 no shutdown
exit
interface Port-channel2
 no switchport
 ip address 10.0.12.1 255.255.255.252
end
```


##### Verify negotiation and membership

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

Look for bundled member flags rather than individual/suspended links. The summary output includes a legend describing flags.

```text
show etherchannel summary
show lacp neighbor
show interfaces Port-channel1
show interfaces Port-channel1 switchport
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- Passive/passive does not initiate LACP.
- One flow generally hashes onto one member; a bundle does not multiply the bandwidth of that individual flow.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

```text
interface range g0/1-2
 switchport mode trunk
 channel-group 1 mode active
interface port-channel 1
 switchport mode trunk
! show etherchannel summary

Layer 3 bundle example (both ends must match):
interface range g0/3-4
 no switchport
 channel-group 2 mode active
interface port-channel 2
 no switchport
 ip address 10.0.12.1 255.255.255.252
! Verify: show etherchannel summary; show interfaces port-channel 2
```


#### Check your understanding

Which LACP pairing forms a bundle?

- **A.** Passive / passive
- **B.** Active / passive
- **C.** On / passive
- **D.** Auto / auto

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**B. Active / passive**

An active LACP endpoint initiates negotiation, and a passive endpoint responds.

</details>

Next objective: [2.5 Rapid PVST+ operation](#objective-2-5)

<a id="objective-2-5"></a>

### 2.5 — Rapid PVST+ operation

**Exam target:** Interpret.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/2.5) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/2.5/commands)

Spanning Tree prevents Layer 2 loops by creating a loop-free forwarding topology. Rapid PVST+ runs a rapid spanning tree per VLAN.

<a id="topic-2-5-a"></a>

#### 2.5.a — Root election and port selection

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/2.5/2.5.a)

The lowest bridge ID wins root election. A nonroot switch selects a root port by total path cost, then tie-breakers such as sender bridge ID and port IDs. Identify designated, alternate and backup ports and use intended primary/secondary root placement rather than accidental MAC order.

<a id="topic-2-5-b"></a>

#### 2.5.b — Rapid spanning-tree roles and states

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/2.5/2.5.b)

RSTP uses discarding, learning and forwarding states. Root/designated ports normally forward while alternate paths provide redundancy. Learning can populate the MAC table without forwarding user frames; a role and a state describe different properties.

<a id="topic-2-5-c"></a>

#### 2.5.c — Rapid forwarding on genuine edge ports

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/2.5/2.5.c)

PortFast accelerates an edge port’s transition to forwarding but does not disable STP. Misusing it between switches can create a temporary loop. Apply it to the intended edge design and use suitable BPDU protection.

<a id="topic-2-5-d"></a>

#### 2.5.d — Guard and filtering behavior

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/2.5/2.5.d)

BPDU guard normally err-disables a protected edge port on BPDU receipt. Root guard can hold a port root-inconsistent after superior BPDUs; loop guard can hold loop-inconsistent if expected BPDUs vanish. BPDU filtering suppresses BPDUs according to its form and can defeat loop protection if misused.

#### Objective overview

- The lowest bridge ID becomes root; bridge ID includes priority, extended system ID, and MAC address. Nonroot switches select a root port using lowest path cost, then tie-breakers. Each segment has a designated port.
- RSTP states are discarding, learning and forwarding. Root and designated ports normally forward; alternate ports provide standby paths. PortFast puts edge ports into forwarding quickly and does not disable STP.
- BPDU guard err-disables an edge port receiving a BPDU. Root guard prevents a port accepting superior BPDUs as a route to a new root. Loop guard prevents inappropriate forwarding when expected BPDUs stop. BPDU filter suppresses BPDUs and can create loops if misused.
- For equal root-path cost, root-port selection compares the sender bridge ID, then sender port ID, and finally the local port ID if still tied. A backup port is an alternate connection to the same shared segment; an alternate port offers another path toward the root. Configure root primary/secondary per VLAN to make the intended topology predictable.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 1 · Chapters 9, 10](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-1-9780138229634)

##### Select the root path in order

Elect the lowest bridge ID per VLAN. A nonroot switch selects the lowest total cost toward the root; ties use sender bridge ID, sender port ID and, if needed, local port ID. Each segment elects a designated port; alternate and backup describe different redundant paths.

##### Distinguish protections

BPDU guard normally err-disables a protected edge port receiving a BPDU. Root guard can hold root-inconsistent on superior BPDUs; loop guard can hold loop-inconsistent when expected BPDUs vanish. BPDU filtering suppresses BPDUs according to its configuration form and can undermine loop prevention.

##### Worked review check

Does PortFast disable spanning tree or make switch-to-switch loops harmless?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

No. It speeds an edge transition while STP remains relevant. A temporary loop can occur when an edge port is misused; apply the appropriate edge design and BPDU protection.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Control the STP root and protect appropriate port roles.

**Covered features:** 2.5a Root/port roles; 2.5b States; 2.5c PortFast; 2.5d Root/loop/BPDU guards and filter.

##### Select primary and secondary roots

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** SW1 primary; SW2 secondary — run the matching section only

Root selection is per VLAN. The macro adjusts bridge priority; verify the resulting root rather than assuming a hostname makes a device primary.

```text
! SW1
enable
configure terminal
spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
spanning-tree vlan 10,20 root primary
end
! SW2
enable
configure terminal
spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
spanning-tree vlan 10,20 root secondary
end
```


##### Protect an endpoint access port

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

Use on an endpoint port. PortFast accelerates forwarding; BPDU guard err-disables the protected port if a BPDU arrives. Do not put this example on a switch-to-switch link.

```text
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1
 switchport mode access
 spanning-tree portfast
 spanning-tree bpduguard enable
end
```


##### Study alternative protections on appropriate links

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

Root guard and loop guard solve different problems and are not combined on the same port here. BPDU filtering suppresses STP visibility: recognize spanning-tree bpdufilter enable, but do not use it to fix a loop.

```text
! Select a downstream port that must never become a root port:
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/23
 spanning-tree guard root
end
! Separate lab link where expected BPDUs must not disappear:
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/22
 spanning-tree guard loop
end
```


##### Interpret root, roles and inconsistent ports

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

Verify the actual root ID, root/designated/alternate roles and forwarding/discarding conditions. Resolve the cause before recovering an err-disabled port.

```text
show spanning-tree vlan 10
show spanning-tree interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1 detail
show spanning-tree inconsistentports
show interfaces status err-disabled
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- Do not use PortFast or BPDU filter as a shortcut on an unexamined inter-switch connection.
- Root/loop guard are selected by the port’s intended role, not enabled indiscriminately.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

```text
spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
spanning-tree vlan 10 root primary
interface g0/10
 spanning-tree portfast
 spanning-tree bpduguard enable
! show spanning-tree vlan 10
```


#### Check your understanding

Which device becomes the STP root bridge?

- **A.** Highest MAC
- **B.** Lowest bridge ID
- **C.** Highest port number
- **D.** Lowest IP

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**B. Lowest bridge ID**

STP elects the lowest bridge ID; priority is compared before the MAC address.

</details>

Next objective: [2.6 Wireless architectures and AP modes](#objective-2-6)

<a id="objective-2-6"></a>

### 2.6 — Wireless architectures and AP modes

**Exam target:** Describe.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/2.6) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/2.6/commands)

Wireless deployments can distribute or centralize management and forwarding decisions.

#### Build your understanding

- Autonomous APs handle configuration locally. Lightweight APs join a WLC using CAPWAP. Cloud-managed APs use a cloud management plane; the data path depends on the architecture.
- In local mode, client data typically tunnels to the controller. FlexConnect can switch client traffic locally at a branch and can support selected functions during WAN outages.
- Other AP modes include monitor for RF analysis and rogue detection, sniffer for packet capture, and bridge modes for wireless links. Use a mode appropriate to the service, because monitoring-only modes do not serve normal clients.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 2 · Chapters 2](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Understand split MAC

Lightweight APs perform time-sensitive radio work while controllers coordinate centralized functions. CAPWAP commonly uses UDP 5246 for control and 5247 for data. User traffic need not always traverse a controller: forwarding depends on architecture and switching policy.

##### Read AP mode first

Local mode normally serves centrally switched clients; FlexConnect can switch locally at a branch. Monitor and sniffer modes are for observation rather than ordinary client service. Autonomous and cloud-managed designs assign control and configuration responsibilities differently.

##### Worked review check

A monitor-mode AP has a reachable management IP. Should normal clients necessarily connect?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

No. Its mode can intentionally exclude ordinary WLAN service. Verify the selected mode and intended client/data-path design.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Inspect a modern controller-based wireless deployment.

**Covered features:** Autonomous/controller/cloud architectures; Local/FlexConnect modes; Monitoring modes.

##### Inspect AP modes and membership

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9800 wireless controller · IOS XE · not AireOS or a switch CLI

Replace AP1 with an actual joined AP. A Catalyst 9800 site tag and Flex profile participate in FlexConnect configuration.

```text
show ap summary
show ap name AP1 config general
show wireless tag site summary
show wireless profile flex summary
```


##### Inspect a branch policy’s switching behavior

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9800 wireless controller · IOS XE · not AireOS or a switch CLI

Read central/local switching settings in the selected policy profile. An AP mode change alone does not supply correct branch VLAN mappings or WAN connectivity.

```text
show wireless profile policy summary
show wireless profile policy detailed BRANCH
show wireless tag policy summary
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- AireOS config ap commands are not Catalyst 9800 IOS XE syntax.
- Full FlexConnect deployment requires site/Flex/policy profiles, tags and an AP assignment; follow the linked controller guide for the specific AP/release.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 9800 controller configuration guides](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/wireless/catalyst-9800-series-wireless-controllers/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

```text
CAPWAP control: UDP 5246
CAPWAP data: UDP 5247
Branch local switching: client → FlexConnect AP → local VLAN → branch gateway
```


#### Check your understanding

Which AP mode supports local switching at a branch?

- **A.** Monitor
- **B.** Sniffer
- **C.** FlexConnect
- **D.** Spectrum-only

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**C. FlexConnect**

FlexConnect supports local switching so branch data can remain at the branch instead of crossing the WAN to the WLC.

</details>

Next objective: [2.7 WLAN component connections](#objective-2-7)

<a id="objective-2-7"></a>

### 2.7 — WLAN component connections

**Exam target:** Describe.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/2.7) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/2.7/commands)

Wireless service depends on both the radio configuration and the wired path carrying management and client traffic.

#### Build your understanding

- An AP port may be an access port when client traffic is centrally tunneled. FlexConnect local switching often needs a trunk for locally switched client VLANs; the correct design determines port configuration.
- WLC uplinks can carry multiple VLANs on 802.1Q trunks and may use link aggregation. A WLAN/SSID is mapped to a client VLAN or policy profile depending on controller generation.
- A controller can connect directly or through switches. Validate PoE, AP management IP, CAPWAP reachability, VLAN allowance, DHCP and gateway paths independently.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 2 · Chapters 2, 4](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Put tags on the intended path

A centrally switched AP can use an access port for management/CAPWAP while the WLC uplink carries client VLANs. FlexConnect local switching may need a trunk at the AP. Port mode follows architecture rather than one universal AP rule.

##### Separate aggregation from mapping

A WLC LAG combines physical links, and the switch-side bundle must agree with supported settings. A trunk transports VLANs; it does not map an SSID to a policy. On 9800, the WLAN, policy profile, policy tag and AP assignment establish that relationship.

##### Worked review check

Only one centrally switched WLAN fails DHCP. Which path should be traced?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

The mapped client VLAN from the controller uplink to its DHCP service or relay. A healthy AP management VLAN does not validate that client path.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Provide the wired path for AP and controller traffic.

**Covered features:** AP access/trunk ports; WLC uplink; LAG; Management/client VLANs.

##### Centrally switched AP on an access port

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

This example is for an AP whose client data is centrally tunneled. VLAN 99 still needs management DHCP/routing/controller reachability. Local-switching FlexConnect may require an AP trunk instead.

```text
enable
configure terminal
vlan 99
 name AP_MANAGEMENT
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/5
 description Centrally_switched_AP
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 99
 spanning-tree portfast
 power inline auto
 no shutdown
end
```


##### Inspect controller uplinks and AP state

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x / Catalyst 9800 wireless controller · IOS XE · not AireOS or a switch CLI

Check native/allowed VLANs and bundle consistency. Configure LACP only if the specific WLC model and deployment support the intended aggregation mode.

```text
! Switch
show interfaces trunk
show etherchannel summary
show power inline
! Controller
show interfaces trunk
show ap summary
show wireless profile policy summary
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- Do not assume every AP port must be a trunk. Match it to the switching design.
- A WLAN-to-VLAN mapping on the WLC does not automatically create that VLAN on every wired switch.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 9800 controller configuration guides](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/wireless/catalyst-9800-series-wireless-controllers/series.html)
- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

```text
SSID Staff → client VLAN 20 → gateway 10.20.0.1
AP management → VLAN 99 → controller reachability
Verify that every required VLAN crosses the intended trunk.
```


#### Check your understanding

An SSID works at Layer 2 but clients get no address. Which service path should be checked?

- **A.** DHCP on the client VLAN
- **B.** STP bridge MAC only
- **C.** Console baud rate
- **D.** NTP stratum only

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**A. DHCP on the client VLAN**

A client needs DHCP reachability in its client VLAN or through a configured relay.

</details>

Next objective: [2.8 Network device management access](#objective-2-8)

<a id="objective-2-8"></a>

### 2.8 — Network device management access

**Exam target:** Describe.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/2.8) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/2.8/commands)

Management access can be in-band through the production network or out-of-band through a separate access path.

#### Build your understanding

- A console gives local access without an IP path. SSH encrypts remote CLI sessions; Telnet exposes credentials and data in plaintext. HTTP is plaintext; HTTPS protects browser-based management with TLS.
- AAA centralizes authentication, authorization and accounting. TACACS+ is commonly used for device administration; RADIUS is common for network access.
- Cloud-managed platforms expose management through a hosted service. Restrict management-plane reachability, use strong identities, and retain an independent recovery path.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 1 · Chapters 4, 6, 16](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-1-9780138229634) · [Volume 2 · Chapters 10](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Know the configuration lifecycle

User/privileged EXEC and global/interface/line configuration modes accept different commands. running-config is active; startup-config supplies saved boot configuration. end exits configuration mode but does not save changes. Save validated changes with copy running-config startup-config.

##### Separate transport and identity

SSH/HTTPS protects a session, while local accounts or AAA govern identity and permissions. Console access can offer an IP-independent recovery path. A Layer 2 management SVI needs an appropriate default gateway; a routing switch uses its routing table.

##### Worked review check

A change works until reboot. What step may be missing?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

Saving validated running-config to startup-config. Also confirm the save succeeded and the device booted the intended configuration.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Use secure management transports.

**Covered features:** Console; SSH/Telnet; HTTPS/HTTP; AAA; Cloud management.

##### Enable SSH with a hashed local lab account

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

Run initially from the console. Replace the placeholder. RSA keys already in use should not be regenerated casually. The account is privileged for a disposable lab; choose least privilege in a real deployment.

```text
enable
configure terminal
hostname SW1
ip domain name lab.example
username learner privilege 15 algorithm-type scrypt secret <REPLACE_WITH_UNIQUE_SECRET>
crypto key generate rsa general-keys modulus 3072
ip ssh version 2
line vty 0 15
 login local
 transport input ssh
 exec-timeout 10 0
end
```


##### Use HTTPS when the WebUI/API is required

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

Use a trusted device certificate and a restricted management path. HTTPS is required by the WebUI/RESTCONF examples; leave the server disabled if your design does not need it.

```text
enable
configure terminal
no ip http server
ip http authentication local
ip http secure-server
end
```


##### Verify access methods and insecure settings

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x

Current IOS XE trains restrict legacy insecure commands. Telnet, plaintext HTTP and weak secrets are exam concepts, not the recommended new configuration. Cloud management is configured through its controller service.

```text
show ip ssh
show ssh
show users
show ip http server status
show system insecure configuration
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- A VTY transport setting is not authentication: verify both login method and SSH key presence.
- Use the actual VTY range present on the device.

##### Command references

- [Cisco C9000 IOS XE resilient infrastructure playbook](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/products/collateral/networking/switches/catalyst-9000-switches/c9000-ios-xe-resilient-infra-pb.html)
- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

```text
ip domain-name lab.example
crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
username admin secret StrongLabPassword
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh
```


#### Check your understanding

Which protocol encrypts a remote CLI session?

- **A.** Telnet
- **B.** SSH
- **C.** TFTP
- **D.** HTTP

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**B. SSH**

SSH protects the remote command session with encryption and authentication.

</details>

Next objective: [2.9 Wireless controller GUI settings](#objective-2-9)

<a id="objective-2-9"></a>

### 2.9 — Wireless controller GUI settings

**Exam target:** Interpret.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/2.9) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/2.9/commands)

A controller GUI ties the visible SSID to security settings, VLAN assignment and policies. Exact menu labels vary by controller family.

#### Build your understanding

- Create a WLAN profile and SSID, enable it, select an interface or policy mapping, and associate the correct client VLAN. A WLAN can exist but remain administratively disabled.
- For WPA2-Personal choose AES/CCMP and a strong pre-shared key. Enterprise security uses 802.1X with a RADIUS server. Verify the intended authentication and encryption suite.
- Check client association, authentication, DHCP address, gateway, and DNS. QoS and advanced WLAN settings should match the application and design; changing RF settings is not the first response to an authentication failure.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 2 · Chapters 4](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Read Catalyst 9800 objects

The WLAN profile defines SSID/security; the policy profile includes client VLAN/policy; a policy tag maps WLAN to policy; and an AP receives that tag. Enable the relevant objects. A correct unassigned WLAN does not establish the configuration actually used by an AP.

##### Recognize AireOS and QoS

AireOS uses dynamic interfaces and WLAN interface mappings rather than the identical 9800 tag model. Read the controller family before following menus. WMM distinguishes voice, video, best effort and background; switching and advanced authentication settings must suit the design.

##### Worked review check

The SSID/PSK works but clients enter the wrong subnet. What relationship matters?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

Inspect the WLAN-to-policy mapping, policy VLAN and AP policy tag on 9800; inspect the WLAN’s dynamic-interface mapping on AireOS.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Connect a WLAN profile, client policy and AP policy tag.

**Covered features:** WLAN creation; Security; QoS profiles; Advanced settings; Client connectivity.

##### Inspect the controller objects behind the GUI

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9800 wireless controller · IOS XE · not AireOS or a switch CLI

GUI path: Configuration → Tags & Profiles. WLANs define SSID/security; policy profiles define client VLAN and policy; policy tags bind them for APs. Lesson 5.10 contains a complete PSK example.

```text
show wlan summary
show wlan name STAFF
show wireless profile policy summary
show wireless profile policy detailed STAFF-POLICY
show wireless tag policy summary
show wireless client summary
```


##### Map an existing WLAN to an existing policy

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9800 wireless controller · IOS XE · not AireOS or a switch CLI

STAFF and STAFF-POLICY must already exist. The tag must be assigned to the intended AP before it advertises the mapped WLAN. This is not the full WLAN deployment by itself.

```text
enable
configure terminal
wireless tag policy LAB-TAG
 wlan STAFF policy STAFF-POLICY
end
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- Inspect client status to distinguish authentication failure from a missing DHCP lease.
- QoS and advanced radio features depend on the controller/AP version; use the GUI and matching release guide, not AireOS screenshots.

- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

```text
GUI checklist:
WLAN enabled → SSID correct → policy/VLAN mapped → WPA2 AES → PSK set → AP advertises WLAN → client connects
```

A WLAN is configured but its SSID is not advertised. Which setting should be checked first?

- **A.** WLAN enabled status
- **B.** NTP authentication
- **C.** OSPF cost

Next objective: [3.1 Routing-table entries](#objective-3-1)

<a id="domain-3-0"></a>

## 3.0 IP Connectivity — 25%

Find the best path with routing tables, static routes, and OSPF.

5 objectives · 18 lettered subtopics

<a id="objective-3-1"></a>

### 3.1 — Routing-table entries

**Exam target:** Interpret.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.1) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.1/commands)

A routing table shows destinations and how the router can reach them. Read the prefix, source, preference, metric, next hop and outgoing interface together.

<a id="topic-3-1-a"></a>

#### 3.1.a — Recognizing the route source

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.1/3.1.a)

Read codes such as C for connected, L for a local interface address, S for static and O for OSPF. The code tells you how the router learned the entry, not whether that entry matches the current packet best.

<a id="topic-3-1-b"></a>

#### 3.1.b — Reading the destination prefix

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.1/3.1.b)

The destination prefix identifies the address block covered by the entry. Use both the network value and prefix length; 10.4.8.0/24 does not match 10.4.9.1 simply because both begin with 10.4.

<a id="topic-3-1-c"></a>

#### 3.1.c — Interpreting the network mask

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.1/3.1.c)

A prefix length or subnet mask marks the significant network bits. A /24 has mask 255.255.255.0, while a /25 covers a smaller block. Do not infer a classful mask when the route provides an explicit CIDR prefix.

<a id="topic-3-1-d"></a>

#### 3.1.d — Resolving the next hop

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.1/3.1.d)

The next-hop address identifies where the packet should go next, possibly requiring a recursive route lookup and ARP/ND resolution. Read the outgoing interface too. A destination route can exist while next-hop resolution or the return path fails.

<a id="topic-3-1-e"></a>

#### 3.1.e — Administrative-distance field

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.1/3.1.e)

In IOS [110/20], 110 is administrative distance. AD ranks different sources competing for the same prefix; lower values are preferred. It does not override longest-prefix forwarding among already installed different prefixes.

<a id="topic-3-1-f"></a>

#### 3.1.f — Protocol metric field

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.1/3.1.f)

In [110/20], 20 is the route metric. Its meaning belongs to the source protocol, such as OSPF cost. Do not directly compare an OSPF metric to another protocol’s differently defined metric.

<a id="topic-3-1-g"></a>

#### 3.1.g — Fallback route selection

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.1/3.1.g)

The gateway of last resort is associated with a default route, 0.0.0.0/0 for IPv4 or ::/0 for IPv6. It is used when no more-specific installed route matches. Without any matching route, the router drops the packet rather than guessing.

#### Objective overview

- IOS route codes include C (connected), L (local), S (static), and O (OSPF). A local route is a host route to the router’s own interface address.
- An entry such as O 10.20.0.0/16 [110/20] via 192.0.2.2 shows administrative distance 110, metric 20 and next hop 192.0.2.2. The outgoing interface and route age may also be shown.
- A default route uses 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0. The gateway of last resort is used only when no more-specific route matches. Network masks in a table need to be interpreted, not inferred from old address classes.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 1 · Chapters 17, 24, 29](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-1-9780138229634)

##### Read every field

C represents a connected prefix; L a local /32 or /128 on the router. S denotes static and O denotes OSPF. Prefix, source, administrative distance, metric, next hop and egress interface answer distinct questions rather than forming one universal preference number.

##### Resolve the next hop

A route may require a second lookup to find its outgoing interface. ARP/ND then supports next-hop delivery on Ethernet. A route in the table does not prove working neighbor resolution, a permissive security policy or a return path.

##### Worked review check

Why can a /32 local route appear beside a connected /24?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

The /32 identifies traffic addressed to the router itself. The /24 identifies the attached subnet used for forwarding to other hosts.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Read IPv4/IPv6 route sources, metrics and next hops.

**Covered features:** Route codes; Prefix/mask; Next hop; AD/metric; Default route.

##### Inspect complete and destination-specific routes

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

Read source code, prefix, [AD/metric], next hop and output interface. A local L route is the router’s own address; connected C routes represent directly connected networks.

```text
show ip route
show ip route 10.20.20.10
show ipv6 route
show ip protocols
```


##### Compare table lookup to forwarding resolution

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

CEF reflects forwarding resolution. A route may exist while an egress adjacency still fails because ARP or the link is broken.

```text
show ip cef 10.20.20.10 detail
show ip arp
show interfaces GigabitEthernet1
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- Do not confuse a static default S* route with every static route in the table.
- The gateway of last resort is used only if there is no more-specific match.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

```text
O 10.20.0.0/16 [110/20] via 192.0.2.2, GigabitEthernet0/0
Source: OSPF | AD: 110 | metric: 20 | next hop: 192.0.2.2
```


#### Check your understanding

In [110/20] on an OSPF route, what is 110?

- **A.** Hop count
- **B.** Administrative distance
- **C.** Prefix length
- **D.** Interface bandwidth

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**B. Administrative distance**

IOS displays administrative distance first and the protocol metric second inside the brackets.

</details>

Next objective: [3.2 Default forwarding decisions](#objective-3-2)

<a id="objective-3-2"></a>

### 3.2 — Default forwarding decisions

**Exam target:** Determine.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.2) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.2/commands)

Separate route installation from packet forwarding. Routing protocols compete to install a route; forwarding then chooses the most-specific matching installed prefix.

<a id="topic-3-2-a"></a>

#### 3.2.a — Selecting the most-specific match

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.2/3.2.a)

Forward a packet using the longest matching installed prefix. A matching /28 beats a /24 even if the /24 came from a source with lower AD. A default /0 is least specific.

<a id="topic-3-2-b"></a>

#### 3.2.b — Comparing competing route sources

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.2/3.2.b)

For the identical prefix, administrative distance chooses between sources. Static AD 1 normally outranks OSPF AD 110 for that prefix. A route with another prefix length can coexist and participate separately in packet lookup.

<a id="topic-3-2-c"></a>

#### 3.2.c — Selecting paths within a protocol

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.2/3.2.c)

The routing protocol’s metric selects its preferred path or equal-cost paths for a destination. For OSPF, compare accumulated costs. Separate this route-selection stage from the later longest-prefix decision for a packet.

#### Objective overview

- For a destination packet, longest prefix match wins: /28 beats /24, which beats /16. A default /0 is least specific.
- For competing routes to the same prefix, lower administrative distance is preferred. Common defaults: connected 0, static 1, eBGP 20, EIGRP internal 90, OSPF 110, RIP 120.
- Within a routing protocol, the protocol’s metric selects the best path. Equal-cost paths can support load balancing. Do not compare OSPF cost directly to another protocol’s metric.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 1 · Chapters 21, 24](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-1-9780138229634)

##### Compare sources for one prefix

For competing identical prefixes, administrative distance ranks route sources and the selected protocol’s metric ranks paths. A static /24 AD 1 can displace an OSPF /24 AD 110. A /25 is a different route and may coexist with the /24.

##### Forward with the longest match

A matching installed /25 wins over an installed /24 even if its source has a higher AD. The packet lookup compares prefix specificity among matching routes. If no route, including a default, matches, the router drops rather than inventing a next hop.

##### Worked review check

Installed routes are 10.0.0.0/8, 10.4.0.0/16 and 10.4.8.0/24. What best matches 10.4.9.1?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

10.4.0.0/16. The /24 for 10.4.8.x does not match this destination at all.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Observe longest prefix match, administrative distance and metric.

**Covered features:** Longest prefix match; Administrative distance; Protocol metric; Equal-cost paths.

##### Create overlapping demonstration routes

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

All three next hops must be reachable. For 10.1.2.55 the installed /24 wins even with AD 200, because it is more specific than the /8 and /16. AD compares candidates for the same prefix.

```text
enable
configure terminal
ip route 10.0.0.0 255.0.0.0 192.0.2.2
ip route 10.1.0.0 255.255.0.0 192.0.2.3
ip route 10.1.2.0 255.255.255.0 192.0.2.4 200
end
```


##### Verify the actual lookup and recursion

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

Resolve the next hop and verify the /24 installed. If a next hop is unreachable, that route may not enter the active table.

```text
show ip route 10.1.2.55
show ip cef 10.1.2.55 detail
show ip route 192.0.2.4
show ip protocols
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- Never compare metric values from different protocols as though they share one unit.
- Use the Route explorer in the practice lab to try additional destinations.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 8000V router documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/routers/catalyst-8000v-edge-software/series.html)
- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

```text
Destination 10.1.2.55
10.0.0.0/8 → A
10.1.2.0/24 → B
10.1.2.48/28 → C
Forward using C: it has the longest matching prefix.
```


#### Check your understanding

A packet matches installed /16 and /24 routes. Which route is used?

- **A.** /16 with lower AD
- **B.** /24
- **C.** Whichever was learned first
- **D.** Neither

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**B. /24**

Longest prefix match selects /24 for forwarding; AD does not override a more-specific installed prefix.

</details>

Next objective: [3.3 IPv4 and IPv6 static routes](#objective-3-3)

<a id="objective-3-3"></a>

### 3.3 — IPv4 and IPv6 static routes

**Exam target:** Configure and verify.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.3) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.3/commands)

Static routes specify a destination prefix and a next hop, outgoing interface, or both. Verify next-hop reachability before expecting traffic to work.

<a id="topic-3-3-a"></a>

#### 3.3.a — Configuring a default path

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.3/3.3.a)

Use an IPv4 0.0.0.0/0 or IPv6 ::/0 static destination for otherwise unmatched traffic. Verify next-hop resolution and the return path. A default does not supersede a matching installed more-specific route.

<a id="topic-3-3-b"></a>

#### 3.3.b — Configuring a subnet or aggregate route

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.3/3.3.b)

A network route covers an aligned prefix rather than one host. Configure the correct mask/prefix and a usable next hop. On Ethernet an IP next hop or fully specified route is clearer than relying on exit-only ARP/proxy-ARP behavior.

<a id="topic-3-3-c"></a>

#### 3.3.c — Configuring a single-host route

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.3/3.3.c)

Use /32 for one IPv4 host and /128 for one IPv6 host. These are more-specific than covering network routes for the same address. Check that the chosen host destination and next-hop reachability are actually correct.

<a id="topic-3-3-d"></a>

#### 3.3.d — Configuring a floating backup

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.3/3.3.d)

A backup static route needs an AD higher than the preferred route to the same prefix. For IPv6 link-local next hops include the outgoing interface. A remote failure that leaves the primary next hop resolvable may require tracking; AD alone is not failure detection.

#### Objective overview

- A network route covers a subnet; a host route uses /32 in IPv4 or /128 in IPv6. A default route matches all otherwise unmatched destinations.
- A floating static route has an administrative distance higher than the preferred route, so it becomes active when the preferred route disappears.
- For an IPv6 link-local next hop, also specify the outgoing interface because link-local addresses have only link scope. On Ethernet, an IP next hop or fully specified route is preferable to an exit-only route.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 1 · Chapters 17, 29](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-1-9780138229634)

##### Choose a next-hop form

IPv4 host routes use /32; IPv6 host routes /128. A link-local IPv6 next hop needs an outgoing interface. On multiaccess Ethernet an exit-only route can create per-destination ARP/proxy-ARP behavior; a reachable next-hop address or fully specified form is usually clearer.

##### Understand backup limits

A floating route needs a higher AD than the preferred route to the same prefix. It activates when the primary is withdrawn or unresolved. A remote failure can leave the primary next hop reachable, requiring tracking in a real design. The backup path also needs a return route.

##### Worked review check

Will a static route AD 5 float behind OSPF AD 110 for the same prefix?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

No. AD 5 is preferred. A backup needs an AD above 110, such as 200, with a usable alternate path.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Configure defaults, network routes, host routes and floating backups.

**Covered features:** IPv4/IPv6; Default; Network; Host; Floating static.

##### Configure IPv4 route variants

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

The route with AD 200 is a backup for the same /16. It installs only when lower-AD candidates disappear; it does not track end-to-end Internet health by itself.

```text
enable
configure terminal
ip route 10.20.0.0 255.255.0.0 192.0.2.2
ip route 192.0.2.80 255.255.255.255 192.0.2.2
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 192.0.2.1
ip route 10.20.0.0 255.255.0.0 198.51.100.2 200
end
```


##### Configure IPv6 route variants

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

A link-local next hop needs its egress interface to disambiguate the link. Replace it with reachable neighbors on that interface.

```text
enable
configure terminal
ipv6 unicast-routing
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 GigabitEthernet1 fe80::2
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::80/128 GigabitEthernet1 fe80::2
ipv6 route ::/0 GigabitEthernet1 fe80::1
! A separate reachable backup link; AD 200 floats above AD 1.
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 GigabitEthernet2 fe80::2 200
end
```


##### Check installation and next-hop reachability

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

Verify both forward and return routing before testing an application.

```text
show ip route static
show ipv6 route static
show ip route 10.20.0.1
show ipv6 neighbors
ping 192.0.2.2
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- An Ethernet exit-interface-only static route can produce undesirable per-destination ARP behavior; use a suitable next hop.
- A high-AD route remaining absent is expected while the primary route is installed.
- A higher AD alone does not detect a remote failure when the primary next hop stays resolvable. Production failover may need tracking and a validated return path.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 8000V router documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/routers/catalyst-8000v-edge-software/series.html)
- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

```text
ip route 10.20.0.0 255.255.0.0 192.0.2.2
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 192.0.2.1
ip route 10.20.0.0 255.255.0.0 198.51.100.2 200
ipv6 route ::/0 g0/0 fe80::1
! show ip route static
```


#### Check your understanding

What makes a static route a floating backup?

- **A.** A lower prefix length
- **B.** An AD higher than the primary route
- **C.** A multicast next hop
- **D.** A loopback source

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**B. An AD higher than the primary route**

The higher administrative distance keeps it out of the active table while the lower-AD route is available.

</details>

Next objective: [3.4 Single-area OSPFv2](#objective-3-4)

<a id="objective-3-4"></a>

### 3.4 — Single-area OSPFv2

**Exam target:** Configure and verify.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.4) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.4/commands)

OSPF is a link-state routing protocol. Routers discover neighbors, synchronize a link-state database and calculate shortest paths using interface costs.

<a id="topic-3-4-a"></a>

#### 3.4.a — Forming and verifying neighbors

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.4/3.4.a)

Check compatible area, addressing where required, timers, authentication and network type. Router IDs must be unique. Read neighbor state: persistent ExStart/Exchange can indicate MTU problems, while two DROthers can legitimately be 2-Way with each other.

<a id="topic-3-4-b"></a>

#### 3.4.b — OSPF on a point-to-point link

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.4/3.4.b)

A point-to-point network type has no DR/BDR election and supports a full adjacency between its two routers. Configure the intended network type consistently and verify it in interface output. A /30 mask alone does not automatically select OSPF point-to-point behavior on Ethernet.

<a id="topic-3-4-c"></a>

#### 3.4.c — Broadcast segments and DR/BDR elections

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.4/3.4.c)

On a broadcast network, eligible routers compare interface priority and then router ID. Priority zero excludes an interface from election. An established election is nonpreemptive; a later higher-priority router does not automatically replace the existing DR.

<a id="topic-3-4-d"></a>

#### 3.4.d — OSPF router identity

[Open this subtopic](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.4/3.4.d)

Prefer an explicit router-id. Otherwise selection normally uses the highest eligible loopback IPv4 address, then the highest eligible nonloopback address at selection time. A router ID is a 32-bit identifier; the local OSPF process number is a different value and need not match neighbors.

#### Objective overview

- Neighbors need compatible area, subnet where required, timers, authentication and network type. MTU problems can prevent database exchange. Router IDs uniquely identify routers; an explicitly configured router ID is predictable.
- On broadcast networks, DR and BDR elections reduce adjacency overhead. Higher interface priority wins, then higher router ID. Priority 0 is ineligible; election is not preemptive. Point-to-point networks need no DR/BDR.
- OSPF cost is based on reference bandwidth divided by interface bandwidth, with a minimum cost of 1. Configure reference bandwidth consistently. Use passive-interface to advertise a connected network without sending hellos there.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 1 · Chapters 21, 22, 23, 24](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-1-9780138229634)

##### Interpret adjacency state

A typical progression is Down, Init, 2-Way, ExStart, Exchange, Loading and Full. Two DROthers on a broadcast network can normally remain 2-Way with each other and Full with DR/BDR. Persistent ExStart/Exchange calls for checks including MTU and network-type compatibility.

##### Know what configuration selects

The process ID is local and need not match neighbors. network statements select local interfaces by address/wildcard and assign an area; ip ospf 1 area 0 is an interface-based alternative. Router ID selection prefers explicit configuration, then highest eligible loopback IPv4, then nonloopback IPv4 at selection time. OSPFv2 uses IP protocol 89, not TCP port 89.

##### Worked review check

Must neighbors using OSPF process 1 and 10 change those numbers to match?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

No. Check actual neighbor requirements such as area, compatible addressing, timers and interface operation. The process ID is a local identifier.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Form and verify a single-area OSPFv2 adjacency.

**Covered features:** Neighbors; Router ID; Point-to-point; Broadcast DR/BDR; Cost/passive interfaces.

##### Configure R1; mirror on R2 with its own addresses

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

R2 uses 10.0.12.2/30 and a distinct router ID 2.2.2.2. Configure point-to-point and the reference bandwidth consistently. Advertise additional LANs with matching network statements; leave their interfaces passive.

```text
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet1
 ip address 10.0.12.1 255.255.255.252
 ip ospf network point-to-point
 no shutdown
exit
router ospf 1
 router-id 1.1.1.1
 auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000
 passive-interface default
 no passive-interface GigabitEthernet1
 network 10.0.12.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
end
```


##### Alternative broadcast-segment election controls

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

This controls eligibility on a broadcast segment; it is not used on the point-to-point link above. A priority of 0 makes a router ineligible. Existing DR/BDR elections are nonpreemptive.

```text
! On a separate broadcast-network lab interface:
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet2
 ip ospf network broadcast
 ip ospf priority 100
end
```


##### Verify adjacency and routes

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

On the point-to-point link expect FULL/-. On broadcast links, some DROTHER neighbors remain 2-WAY with each other as part of normal operation.

```text
show ip ospf neighbor
show ip ospf interface brief
show ip ospf interface GigabitEthernet1
show ip protocols
show ip route ospf
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- Check subnet, area, timers, authentication, MTU, network type and passive status on both ends.
- Changing a router ID may require restarting the OSPF process; that interrupts adjacencies and is not needed for this initial configuration.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 8000V router documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/routers/catalyst-8000v-edge-software/series.html)
- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

```text
router ospf 1
 router-id 1.1.1.1
 network 10.0.12.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
 passive-interface g0/1
! show ip ospf neighbor
! show ip route ospf
```


#### Check your understanding

On a broadcast OSPF segment, which router is preferred as DR?

- **A.** Lowest router ID always
- **B.** Highest priority, then highest router ID
- **C.** Lowest interface IP always
- **D.** Newest neighbor

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**B. Highest priority, then highest router ID**

Eligible routers compare interface priority first, then router ID. Existing DR elections are nonpreemptive.

</details>

Next objective: [3.5 First-hop redundancy concepts](#objective-3-5)

<a id="objective-3-5"></a>

### 3.5 — First-hop redundancy concepts

**Exam target:** Describe.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.5) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/3.5/commands)

Hosts normally configure one default gateway. FHRPs preserve a stable virtual gateway while the physical forwarding router can change.

#### Build your understanding

- HSRP uses an active router and a standby router. VRRP uses a master (called active in newer terminology) and backups. They provide a shared virtual IP and MAC to clients.
- If the active gateway fails, another router takes over the virtual identity. The client need not change its configured gateway or know which physical router is forwarding.
- Priority influences the active router; preemption allows a higher-priority router to take over where supported and configured. Interface tracking can reduce priority when an upstream link fails. FHRP does not replace a routing protocol.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 2 · Chapters 16](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Follow the virtual identity

A client resolves the virtual gateway IP to a virtual MAC. HSRP changes which router forwards for that identity. Preemption controls whether a recovered higher-priority router retakes the role. Tracking can reduce priority after an upstream failure while the client-facing link remains up.

##### Compare protocol families

VRRP elects an active/master role and backups. GLBP can give different virtual MACs to clients for load sharing. FHRP protects the first hop; it does not replace resilient routing and upstream connectivity. Conceptual comparison is useful even when full deployment is outside the blueprint verb.

##### Worked review check

Why can clients be blackholed after only the active gateway’s upstream fails?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

Without suitable tracking/failure detection, that router may retain the active role. A healthy client-facing interface alone does not prove upstream reachability.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Provide a virtual first-hop gateway using HSRP.

**Covered features:** FHRP purpose; Virtual IP/MAC; Active/standby; Priority/preemption.

##### Configure R1 as the preferred gateway

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

Configure R2 on the same LAN as .3 with the same virtual .1 and group 10, priority 100, and preempt. Clients use the virtual .1, not a physical router address.

```text
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet1
 ip address 10.10.10.2 255.255.255.0
 standby version 2
 standby 10 ip 10.10.10.1
 standby 10 priority 110
 standby 10 preempt
 no shutdown
end
```


##### Inspect active/standby state

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

HSRP support depends on platform and license. Verify one active and one standby, and test a controlled failure in a disposable lab.

```text
show standby brief
show standby GigabitEthernet1
show ip arp
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- A shared virtual gateway does not supply upstream routes or fix a failed Internet path.
- Preemption and interface tracking affect failover; choose tracking rules according to the topology.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 8000V router documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/routers/catalyst-8000v-edge-software/series.html)
- [Catalyst 9300 configuration and command references](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/switches/catalyst-9300-series-switches/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

```text
Client default gateway: 10.10.10.1 (virtual)
Router A: 10.10.10.2 → active
Router B: 10.10.10.3 → standby
Failure of A → B assumes virtual gateway.
```


#### Check your understanding

What address should clients normally use with an FHRP?

- **A.** The standby physical address
- **B.** The virtual gateway IP
- **C.** The multicast group IP
- **D.** The router ID

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**B. The virtual gateway IP**

The virtual IP remains stable even when the active physical gateway changes.

</details>

### 4.1 — Inside-source NAT: static mappings and pools

**Exam target:** Configure and verify.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/4.1) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/4.1/commands)

NAT rewrites addresses at a boundary. Inside local identifies the inside host as seen internally; inside global is its translated identity outside.

#### Build your understanding

- Static NAT creates a fixed one-to-one mapping. Dynamic NAT assigns a mapping from a pool while translations are in use; pool exhaustion can prevent new mappings.
- Mark inside and outside interfaces and define which inside sources are eligible. A NAT classification ACL selects traffic for translation; it is not automatically a security filter.
- PAT (overload) allows many inside sessions to share a global address by tracking transport ports. Verify translations, interface roles, routing, and the classification ACL together.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 2 · Chapters 14](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Read local and global correctly

Inside local describes the inside host internally; inside global describes its translated external identity. A dynamic pool without overload needs an available global address for each simultaneously translated inside address. PAT distinguishes flows sharing a global address using transport information.

##### Validate both directions

Inspect inside/outside roles, classification, translations created by real test traffic and return routing. A NAT ACL selects translation; denying translation does not automatically drop a packet. Clearing stale translations can affect active sessions and needs appropriate lab scope.

##### Worked review check

A dynamic pool has ten global addresses without overload. Why might an eleventh active host fail?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

There may be no free one-to-one mapping. Check pool utilization and whether the intended design needs more addresses or suitable PAT.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Translate private addresses on a NAT-capable router.

**Covered features:** Static NAT; Dynamic NAT pool; PAT overload; Inside local/global.

##### Mark inside/outside and create a static mapping

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

The upstream network must deliver the translated address to this router. Documentation addresses represent a closed lab, not real public Internet allocation.

```text
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet1
 ip address 10.0.0.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat inside
 no shutdown
exit
interface GigabitEthernet2
 ip address 203.0.113.2 255.255.255.0
 ip nat outside
 no shutdown
exit
ip nat inside source static 10.0.0.10 203.0.113.10
end
```


##### Alternative: dynamic pool or PAT — choose one for the test sources

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

Do not leave competing source rules active for this same demonstration. PAT shares the outside interface address using session port information.

```text
enable
configure terminal
ip access-list standard NAT-SOURCES
 permit 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255
exit
! Dynamic one-to-one pool example:
ip nat pool PUBLIC 203.0.113.20 203.0.113.30 netmask 255.255.255.0
ip nat inside source list NAT-SOURCES pool PUBLIC
end
! PAT alternative: remove the preceding dynamic rule first.
configure terminal
no ip nat inside source list NAT-SOURCES pool PUBLIC
ip nat inside source list NAT-SOURCES interface GigabitEthernet2 overload
end
```


##### Generate client traffic, then inspect translations

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

Dynamic translations appear after matching inside-host traffic. A router-originated ping may not exercise the same inside-to-outside NAT path.

```text
show ip nat translations
show ip nat statistics
show ip access-lists NAT-SOURCES
show ip route
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- NAT is not available on every Catalyst switch; use the labeled router platform.
- A NAT classification ACL selects translations; it is not automatically an interface security filter.

##### Command references

- [Catalyst 8000V router documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/routers/catalyst-8000v-edge-software/series.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

```text
interface g0/0
 ip nat inside
interface g0/1
 ip nat outside
ip nat inside source static 10.0.0.10 203.0.113.10
! Dynamic pool:
ip nat pool PUBLIC 203.0.113.20 203.0.113.30 netmask 255.255.255.0
access-list 1 permit 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255
ip nat inside source list 1 pool PUBLIC
! show ip nat translations
```


#### Check your understanding

Which NAT type creates a fixed one-to-one address mapping?

- **A.** Static NAT
- **B.** DHCP
- **C.** DNS caching
- **D.** OSPF

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**A. Static NAT**

Static NAT permanently associates a chosen inside local address with an inside global address.

</details>

Next objective: [4.2 NTP clients and servers](#objective-4-2)

<a id="objective-4-2"></a>

### 4.2 — NTP clients and servers

**Exam target:** Configure and verify.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/4.2) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/4.2/commands)

NTP synchronizes device clocks, which is essential for meaningful logs, certificate checks and incident analysis.

#### Build your understanding

- An NTP client synchronizes to an upstream server, normally over UDP 123. A device can also serve time to downstream clients.
- Stratum describes distance from a reference clock. A reference source is stratum 0; a directly attached server is stratum 1. A lower stratum does not by itself guarantee a trustworthy source.
- Configure reliable reachable sources, secure time distribution according to policy, and verify association state and synchronization. A wrong timezone affects display, while NTP operates on a common time base.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition

Suggested reading: [Volume 2 · Chapters 13](https://www.ciscopress.com/store/ccna-200-301-official-cert-guide-volume-2-9780138214951)

##### Read association state

Inspect peer selection, reachability, offset and synchronized status. Strata 1–15 describe synchronized hierarchy levels; stratum 16 indicates an unsynchronized condition. An NTP server can itself be an upstream client, and a low stratum is not a trust guarantee.

##### Separate time display from reference

Timezone changes local display, not synchronization. A lab ntp master can distribute a wrong clock consistently if treated as an authoritative source. Match supported authentication and access policy at both endpoints and verify the reference itself.

##### Worked review check

Can devices agree on time and all be wrong?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

Yes. They may be synchronized to the same inaccurate source. Agreement among clients does not establish reference accuracy.

</details>

#### Platform-labeled command guide

Synchronize a client and understand server mode.

**Covered features:** NTP client; NTP server; Stratum; Verification.

##### Configure authenticated upstream time

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x or IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

The server must support the same key ID, algorithm and secret. Use the parser on your image to confirm accepted key encoding; do not use legacy MD5 to work around a current-release restriction.

```text
enable
configure terminal
ntp authenticate
ntp authentication-key 10 hmac-sha2-256 <SHARED_NTP_KEY>
ntp trusted-key 10
ntp server 192.0.2.123 key 10
end
```


##### Dedicated isolated-lab time source — optional

**Category:** configure. **Platform/context:** IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

Run only on the separate lab device intended to serve as an unsynchronized local reference. This is not a trustworthy UTC source for a real network; use a suitable upstream reference instead.

```text
enable
configure terminal
ntp master 8
end
```


##### Verify association and synchronization

**Category:** verify. **Platform/context:** Catalyst 9300 switch · IOS XE 26.x or IOS XE router · Catalyst 8000V/8000 lab · feature/license support required

Allow time for synchronization. Association output identifies the selected peer; matching keys alone do not prove that its clock is correct.

```text
show ntp associations
show ntp status
show clock detail
```


##### Troubleshooting checks

- Check routing, UDP 123, source addresses and the matching authentication settings.
- Timezone settings alter displayed local time; NTP synchronizes a common time base.

##### Command references

- [Administering the device — IOS XE 26.x](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/td/docs/switches/lan/catalyst9300/software/release/26-x/configuration_guide/sys_mgmt/b_26x_sys_mgmt_9300_cg/administering_the_device.html)
- [Cisco C9000 IOS XE resilient infrastructure playbook](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/products/collateral/networking/switches/catalyst-9000-switches/c9000-ios-xe-resilient-infra-pb.html)
- [Cisco IOS XE 26 release documentation](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/ios-nx-os-software/ios-xe-26/series.html)

#### Additional concept example

This may use older IOS syntax or an illustrative text diagram. Use the platform-labeled guide above for the intended current lab context.

```text
ntp server 192.0.2.123
! Lab-only local time source when no upstream exists:
! ntp master 8
show ntp associations
show ntp status
show clock detail
```


#### Check your understanding

Which UDP port does NTP use?

- **A.** 53
- **B.** 67
- **C.** 123
- **D.** 161

<details>
<summary>Answer and explanation</summary>

**C. 123**

NTP uses UDP port 123.

</details>

Next objective: [4.3 DHCP and DNS roles](#objective-4-3)

<a id="objective-4-3"></a>

### 4.3 — DHCP and DNS roles

**Exam target:** Explain.

[Open objective](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/4.3) · [Open command guide](https://ianlin-smci.github.io/ccna-study-lab/#/lesson/4.3/commands)

DHCP supplies host configuration; DNS maps names to records. They solve different problems and can fail independently.

#### Build your understanding

- IPv4 DHCP commonly follows Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge (DORA). Servers use UDP 67 and clients UDP 68. Options include subnet mask, gateway, DNS servers and lease duration.
- DNS A records map names to IPv4 addresses; AAAA to IPv6; CNAME aliases names; MX identifies mail service; PTR supports reverse lookup. DNS commonly uses UDP and TCP 53.
- A DHCP relay forwards client requests across a routed boundary. DNS recursion obtains answers on a client’s behalf; cached records remain valid according to their TTL.

#### Supporting reading — Official Cert Guide, Second Edition
